newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew to test new Earth link, talk to families.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew to test new Earth link, talk to families.

text.p: The crew aboard the crippled space station Mir is expected on Saturday to test new equipment giving them better radio and television links with Earth ahead of vital repairs next week, an official said.

The ageing space station has lost about half of its power since a Russian supply craft collided with it on June 25, and clearer radio, television and data reception will help the crew as they plan repairs with Mission Control scheduled for the early morning hours of July 18.
"Today is a normal working day," spokesman Vladislav Tachilo said at Mission Control outside Moscow. "This evening they will test the new Antares transmitters."

The new transmitters were part of a cargo shipment sent up earlier this week that included supplies to repair the solar panels in the damaged Spektr module and seal it off from the rest of the space station.
The transmitters will also facilitate a video link between the crew of two Russians and one British-American and their families, who will have a chance to talk privately on Sunday, Tachilo said.
"When the wives speak to their husbands, all the transmitters in Mission Control are shut off," he said. "Their talks will be private."
Although the crew was clearly tense and under great pressure in the days immediately after the accident, Tachilo said they had relaxed since then. "They're in good spirits," he said.
Earlier this week, American astronaut Michael Foale, who has a doctorate in laboratory astrophysics, said he missed not finding out more about the U.S. probe now on Mars.
"The most frustrating thing is I haven't seen a picture from Mars yet," he said.

At Mir Mission Control the atmosphere was low-key and relaxed on Saturday, as many officials apparently took the day off ahead of a tense week that is likely to determine the future of the 11-year-old orbiting station. The sole guard at the entrance to the building was absent from her post when a reporter arrived.

On Tuesday, the crew plans a dress rehearsal of their difficult repair job, which involves donning space suits inside the Mir and practising linking up 17 internal cables to the solar panels attached to the Spektr's exterior.
The Spektr has been sealed off from the rest of the space station since it suffered a puncture in the June 25 accident.

During the repairs a cosmonaut will also install a new hatch separating the Spektr from the Mir's other cluttered array of modules. Unlike the old hatch, the new version can be closed without requiring the cables to the solar panels to be unplugged.

But the repair is expected to be difficult as the Russian cosmonaut doing the work, with a second in reserve nearby, will be dressed in a bulky spacesuit and be operating in a cramped interior area of the station, space officials say.
